messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Caleb Hartwell is a 29-year-old single man of North American descent who works as a jeweler in a small independent shop in his hometown. He came to the intake appointment wearing a jacket despite the warm weather, choosing a chair in the far corner of the waiting room with his back pressed firmly against the wall — a posture that, as he would later explain, had become as automatic as breathing. He was referred for assessment following a period of escalating distress that had begun roughly eighteen months earlier, after returning from a fourteen-month deployment as a relief worker in an active conflict zone in the Middle East.

During his deployment, Caleb had worked in a field distribution center providing medical supplies and food to displaced families. In the final weeks of his posting, the compound came under sustained mortar fire during a distribution event. He remembers the moment the first shell landed: the concussive thud that travelled through the ground and into his chest, the sudden cacophony of children screaming in the crowd, the press of panicked bodies against him as people surged in every direction. A colleague grabbed his arm without warning to pull him toward cover, and the unexpected contact sent a bolt of pure terror through him before he understood what was happening. He spent the next several hours pinned behind a concrete barrier, his heart hammering so violently he was certain he was dying, listening to the cries of injured children he could not reach. Three children in the crowd were killed. Caleb was physically unharmed.

Since returning, his body has retained the event in ways that ambush him without permission. The sound of a child crying — in a supermarket, on the street outside the jewelry shop — can instantly collapse the distance between present and past, delivering the full sensory weight of that afternoon without any transitional warning. The memories that surface are not dim or dreamlike; they carry a vividness and physical immediacy that makes his ordinary recollections of childhood or last week feel pale and insubstantial by comparison. Sometimes there is no image at all, only the dread — a wave of grief and terror arriving from nowhere, sourceless, which he finds in some ways more disorienting than the full flashback. His own heart racing, whether from climbing stairs or drinking too much coffee, is among the most reliable of these portals: the moment he feels that familiar pounding, his nervous system interprets it as evidence that something is already wrong, and the memories crowd in before he can stop them.

Because the memories arrive with such force, Caleb has developed a set of strategies he believes are keeping him functional. He forces himself to think only positive thoughts when distress rises, and reminds himself — repeatedly, almost ritually — that it could have been worse, that he survived, that others suffered more. These efforts at reframing do briefly interrupt the emotional intensity, but they also require him to actively suppress the content of what he lived through, which means the memories never settle or integrate; they remain pressurised, and the next trigger finds them just as raw. The suppression itself seems to prime the system: after a session of forced positivity, he finds his mind scanning more urgently for the next threat, as though the effort of containment has heightened his vigilance rather than reduced it. That vigilance — the constant environmental scanning, the cataloguing of every potentially dangerous object within reach, the inability to sit with his back exposed — keeps him in a state of sustained physiological readiness that makes his heart race, which in turn reopens the memory, completing a circuit he cannot find the exit from. When others tell him he is safe, he recognises intellectually that they mean well, but he cannot make himself believe it; the threat feels too structurally present to be dismissed by reassurance.

In his daily work at the jewelry shop, the layout of the workspace has quietly reorganised itself around his needs. He rearranged the back workbench so that it faces the door, and he has asked his employer not to approach him from behind. Customers who reach across the counter unexpectedly sometimes trigger a visible startle response that he finds humiliating to explain. He has stopped attending the monthly jewelers' guild meetings because the crowded room, with its unpredictable movement and noise, is unmanageable.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a moment last month when a child in the shop began crying after dropping a bracelet, and he found himself crouched behind the display case, shaking, unable to stand. He is most afraid that what happened to him has permanently altered something fundamental — that the person who left for that deployment no longer exists. What he is hoping for, quietly and with some embarrassment, is simply to be able to do his job without bracing for the world to end.
